      <![CDATA[<p>”To the Best of Our Knowledge” is a <a href="http://www.peabodyawards.com/award-profile/to-the-best-of-our-knowledge"><strong>Peabody award-winning</strong></a> national public radio show that explores big ideas and beautiful questions. Deep interviews with philosophers, writers, artists, scientists, historians, and others help listeners find new sources of meaning, purpose, and wonder in daily life. Whether it’s about bees, poetry, skin, or psychedelics, every episode is an intimate, sound-rich journey into open-minded, open-hearted conversations. Warm and engaging, TTBOOK helps listeners feel less alone and more connected – to our common humanity and to the world we share.</p><p>For more from the TTBOOK team, visit us at <a href="https://ttbook.org"><strong>ttbook.org.</strong></a></p>]]>

      <![CDATA[”To the Best of Our Knowledge” is a <a href="http://www.peabodyawards.com/award-profile/to-the-best-of-our-knowledge">Peabody award-winning</a> national public radio show that explores big ideas and beautiful questions. Deep interviews with philosophers, writers, artists, scientists, historians, and others help listeners find new sources of meaning, purpose, and wonder in daily life. Whether it’s about bees, poetry, skin, or psychedelics, every episode is an intimate, sound-rich journey into open-minded, open-hearted conversations. Warm and engaging, TTBOOK helps listeners feel less alone and more connected – to our common humanity and to the world we share.

For more from the TTBOOK team, visit us at <a href="https://ttbook.org">ttbook.org.</a>]]>

Nature writers and darkness activists tell us what we’re missing.<br><br><a href="http://ttbook.org/deeptime"><strong><em>Deep Time</em></strong></a><em> is a series all about the natural ecologies of time from To The Best Of Our Knowledge and the </em><a href="http://humansandnature.org/kinship"><strong><em>Center for Humans and Nature</em></strong></a><em>. We'll explore life beyond the clock, develop habits of "timefulness" and learn how to live with greater awareness of the many types of time in our lives.</em></p><p><em>Original Air Date: December 21, 2024</em></p><p><strong>Interviews In This Hour: </strong><br><a href="https://www.ttbook.org/interview/listening-song-night"><strong>Listening to the song of the night</strong></a> — <a href="https://www.ttbook.org/interview/adjusting-our-eyes-wonders-nocturnal-world"><strong>Adjusting our eyes to wonders of the nocturnal world</strong></a></p><p><strong>Guests: </strong><br><a href="https://www.ttbook.org/people/sam-lee"><strong>Sam Lee</strong></a>, <a href="https://www.ttbook.org/people/leigh-ann-henion"><strong>Leigh Ann Henion</strong></a></p><p><br><em>Never want to miss an episode?</em> <a href="https://link.chtbl.com/TTBOOK"><strong>Subscribe to the podcast.</strong></a><br><em>Want to hear more from us, including extended interviews and favorites from the archive? </em><a href="https://ttbook.us11.list-manage.com/subscribe/post?u=3cb4c021b28e511db7dc0b1ca&amp;id=64562fd7d9"><strong>Subscribe to our newsletter.</strong></a></p>]]>

        <![CDATA[The longest nights of the year are here, but how many of us will see them? The global spread of light pollution is making it harder to experience dark skies and natural darkness. Learning how to reconnect with the planet’s ancient nocturnal rhythms can be profoundly restorative. Nature writers and darkness activists tell us what we’re missing.

<a href="http://ttbook.org/deeptime">Deep Time</a> is a series all about the natural ecologies of time from To The Best Of Our Knowledge and the <a href="http://humansandnature.org/kinship">Center for Humans and Nature</a>. We'll explore life beyond the clock, develop habits of "timefulness" and learn how to live with greater awareness of the many types of time in our lives.

Original Air Date: December 21, 2024

Interviews In This Hour:
<a href="https://www.ttbook.org/interview/listening-song-night">Listening to the song of the night</a> — <a href="https://www.ttbook.org/interview/adjusting-our-eyes-wonders-nocturnal-world">Adjusting our eyes to wonders of the nocturnal world</a>

Guests:
<a href="https://www.ttbook.org/people/sam-lee">Sam Lee</a>, <a href="https://www.ttbook.org/people/leigh-ann-henion">Leigh Ann Henion</a>

      <title>Island of Knowledge: What is Life?</title>
      <pubDate>Sat, 12 Jul 2025 11:00:00 -0000</pubDate>
      <link>https://www.ttbook.org/show/island-knowledge-what-life</link>

        <![CDATA[It’s summer, and you might be pulling out your binoculars, filling your bird feeders, and looking up as you hear a melodious song. But for many birdwatchers, it's not just a simple pastime.         <![CDATA[How does someone become an official saint?  Meet Dorothy Day — journalist, radical activist, mother and lay minister to the poor who died in 1980 — who is being considered for sainthood by the Catholic Church.         <![CDATA[Music crosses boundaries between traditional and modern, local and global, personal and political. Take jazz — a musical form born out of forced migration and enslavement. We typically think it originated in New Orleans and then spread around the world. But today, we examine an alternate history of jazz — one that starts in Africa, then crisscrosses the planet, following the movements of people and empires -- from colonial powers to grassroots revolutionaries to contemporary artists throughout the diaspora.

This history of jazz is like the music itself: fluid and improvisatory.  

In this hour, produced in partnership with the <a href="https://chcinetwork.org/">Consortium of Humanities Centers and Institutes (CHCI)</a> — a global consortium of 270 humanities centers and institutes — we hear how both African and African-American music have shaped the sound of the world today.

 

Original Air Date: July 04, 2020

        <![CDATA[<p>Most Americans take their sovereignty for granted — the nation’s right to make its own laws and govern its own people. It’s an ongoing, daily struggle. </p><p><em>Original Air Date: July 13, 2024</em></p><p><strong>Interviews In This Hour: </strong><br><a href="https://www.ttbook.org/interview/battle-over-tribal-rights-bad-river"><strong>The battle over tribal rights in Bad River</strong></a> — <a href="https://www.ttbook.org/interview/quannah-chasinghorses-two-worlds-native-activist-and-supermodel"><strong>Quannah ChasingHorse’s two worlds – Native activist and supermodel</strong></a> — <a href="https://www.ttbook.org/interview/are-indian-casinos-key-tribal-sovereignty"><strong>Are Indian casinos the key to tribal sovereignty?</strong></a> — <a href="https://www.ttbook.org/interview/no-more-native-american-trauma-porn"><strong>No more Native American 'trauma porn'</strong></a></p><p><strong>Guests: </strong><br><a href="https://www.ttbook.org/people/mary-mazzio"><strong>Mary Mazzio</strong></a>, <a href="https://www.ttbook.org/people/quannah-chasinghorse"><strong>Quannah ChasingHorse</strong></a>, <a href="https://www.ttbook.org/people/steven-andrew-light"><strong>Steven Andrew Light</strong></a>, <a href="https://www.ttbook.org/people/david-treuer"><strong>David Treuer</strong></a></p><p><br><em>Never want to miss an episode?</em> <a href="https://link.chtbl.com/TTBOOK"><strong>Subscribe to the podcast.</strong></a><br><em>Want to hear more from us, including extended interviews and favorites from the archive? </em><a href="https://ttbook.us11.list-manage.com/subscribe/post?u=3cb4c021b28e511db7dc0b1ca&amp;id=64562fd7d9"><strong>Subscribe to our newsletter.</strong></a></p>]]>

She is a member of the Bad River Band of Lake Superior Ojibwe.</li>

<li>Activist Suzan Shown Harjo is the recipient of a <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=28aiDWgxXdU"><strong>2014 Presidential Medal of Freedom</strong></a>. She is Cheyenne and Hodulgee Muscogee.</li>
<li>Patty Loew is the director of the <a href="https://www.northwestern.edu/native-american-and-indigenous-peoples/people/cnair.html"><strong>Center for Native American and Indigenous Research</strong></a> at Northwestern University. She is a member of the Bad River Band of Lake Superior Ojibwe.</li>
</ul><p><em>Special thanks to Robert W. Wheeler and the Smithsonian for archival audio.</em></p><p><em>Original Air Date: January 14, 2023</em></p><p><strong>Interviews In This Hour: </strong><br><a href="https://www.ttbook.org/interview/was-jim-thorpe-greatest-athlete-who-ever-lived"><strong>Was Jim Thorpe the greatest athlete who ever lived?</strong></a> — <a href="https://www.ttbook.org/interview/white-mans-trophy"><strong>The white man's trophy</strong></a> — <a href="https://www.ttbook.org/interview/hero-who-looks-me"><strong>A hero who looks like me</strong></a> — <a href="https://www.ttbook.org/interview/indigenous-excellence-hip-hop-and-legacy-jim-thorpe"><strong>Indigenous excellence: Hip hop and the legacy of Jim Thorpe</strong></a></p><p><strong>Guests: </strong><br><a href="https://www.ttbook.org/people/tall-paul"><strong>Tall Paul</strong></a>, <a href="https://www.ttbook.org/people/suzan-shown-harjo"><strong>Suzan Shown Harjo</strong></a>, <a href="https://www.ttbook.org/people/patty-loew"><strong>Patty Loew</strong></a>, <a href="https://www.ttbook.org/people/david-maraniss"><strong>David Maraniss</strong></a></p><p><br><em>Never want to miss an episode?</em> <a href="https://link.chtbl.com/TTBOOK"><strong>Subscribe to the podcast.</strong></a><br><em>Want to hear more from us, including extended interviews and favorites from the archive? </em><a href="https://ttbook.us11.list-manage.com/subscribe/post?u=3cb4c021b28e511db7dc0b1ca&amp;id=64562fd7d9"><strong>Subscribe to our newsletter.</strong></a></p>]]>

Nature writers and darkness activists tell us what we’re missing.<br><br><a href="http://ttbook.org/deeptime"><strong><em>Deep Time</em></strong></a><em> is a series all about the natural ecologies of time from To The Best Of Our Knowledge and the </em><a href="http://humansandnature.org/kinship"><strong><em>Center for Humans and Nature</em></strong></a><em>.         <![CDATA[The longest nights of the year are here, but how many of us will see them? The global spread of light pollution is making it harder to experience dark skies and natural darkness. Learning how to reconnect with the planet’s ancient nocturnal rhythms can be profoundly restorative. Nature writers and darkness activists tell us what we’re missing.

<a href="http://ttbook.org/deeptime">Deep Time</a> is a series all about the natural ecologies of time from To The Best Of Our Knowledge and the <a href="http://humansandnature.org/kinship">Center for Humans and Nature</a>. We'll explore life beyond the clock, develop habits of "timefulness" and learn how to live with greater awareness of the many types of time in our lives.

Original Air Date: December 21, 2024

Interviews In This Hour:
<a href="https://www.ttbook.org/interview/listening-song-night">Listening to the song of the night</a> — <a href="https://www.ttbook.org/interview/adjusting-our-eyes-wonders-nocturnal-world">Adjusting our eyes to wonders of the nocturnal world</a>

So what are they writing about today?</p><p><em>This episode was produced in partnership with the </em><a href="https://economichardship.org/"><strong><em>Economic Hardship Reporting Project</em></strong></a><em>.</em></p><p><em>Original Air Date: January 13, 2024</em></p><p><strong>Interviews In This Hour: </strong><br><a href="https://www.ttbook.org/interview/gospel-suncere-ali-shakur"><strong>The gospel of Suncere Ali Shakur</strong></a> — <a href="https://www.ttbook.org/interview/how-i-drew-you"><strong>This is how I drew you</strong></a> — <a href="https://www.ttbook.org/interview/poetry-bears-witness-everyday"><strong>The poetry that bears witness to the everyday</strong></a></p><p><strong>Guests: </strong><br><a href="https://www.ttbook.org/people/philip-metres"><strong>Philip Metres</strong></a>, <a href="https://www.ttbook.org/people/suncere-ali-shakur"><strong>Suncere Ali Shakur</strong></a>, <a href="https://www.ttbook.org/people/kaia-sand"><strong>Kaia Sand</strong></a>, <a href="https://www.ttbook.org/people/camille-dungy"><strong>Camille Dungy</strong></a></p><p><br><em>Never want to miss an episode?</em> <a href="https://link.chtbl.com/TTBOOK"><strong>Subscribe to the podcast.</strong></a><br><em>Want to hear more from us, including extended interviews and favorites from the archive? </em><a href="https://ttbook.us11.list-manage.com/subscribe/post?u=3cb4c021b28e511db7dc0b1ca&amp;id=64562fd7d9"><strong>Subscribe to our newsletter.</strong></a></p>]]>

        <![CDATA[How we live is indelibly intertwined with the care and empathy we give to each other. What if we put care into helping Americans find homes and build dwellings, into keeping their bodies and minds sound, and finding meaningful and well-paid work? <a href="https://ttbook.org/goingforbroke">In this three part series</a>, "<a href="http://ttbook.org/">To The Best Of Our Knowledge</a>" and the <a href="http://economichardship.org/">Economic Hardship Reporting Project </a>bring you real life stories about economic struggle in our time, as well as ideas for solutions. 

Post-traumatic stress disorder and other mental health challenges can push people into poverty. Meanwhile, the experience of financial desperation can also create even more trauma, even more suffering. How do you break the cycle? How do we truly care for people mentally and financially?

If you or someone you know are having mental health struggles, we wanted to make sure you are aware of some resources. <a href="https://nicic.gov/national-suicide-prevention-lifeline">The National Suicide and Crisis Lifeline</a> is available 24 hours a day by calling 9-8-8. <a href="https://www.nami.org/Home">The National Alliance on Mental Illness </a>reminds us that one in five people in the US has a mental health concern every year. You can find support and education at their web site, <a href="https://www.nami.org/Home">nami.org</a>.

      <title>Luminous: Can psychedelics be decolonized?</title>
      <pubDate>Sat, 06 Jul 2024 11:00:00 -0000</pubDate>
      <link>https://www.ttbook.org/show/luminous-can-psychedelics-be-decolonized</link>

        <![CDATA[<p>It’s easy to get caught up in the hype about how psychedelics might revolutionize the treatment of mental illness. But there are also lots of ethical concerns.         <![CDATA[It’s easy to get caught up in the hype about how psychedelics might revolutionize the treatment of mental illness. But there are also lots of ethical concerns. And probably none are so troubling as the charges of exploitation and cultural appropriation. The fact is, the knowledge about many psychedelics — like magic mushrooms and ayahuasca — comes from the sacred ceremonies of Indigenous cultures. <li>Activist Suzan Shown Harjo is the recipient of a <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=28aiDWgxXdU"><strong>2014 Presidential Medal of Freedom</strong></a>. She is Cheyenne and Hodulgee Muscogee.</li>
<li>Patty Loew is the director of the <a href="https://www.northwestern.edu/native-american-and-indigenous-peoples/people/cnair.html"><strong>Center for Native American and Indigenous Research</strong></a> at Northwestern University. She is a member of the Bad River Band of Lake Superior Ojibwe.</li>

        <![CDATA[Jim Thorpe was one of the greatest athletes the world has ever known — a legend in the NFL, MLB, NCAA, and in the Olympics. Today he is being celebrated by a new generation of Native Americans. 

Rapper Tall Paul’s album is called, “<a href="https://tallpaulhiphop.bandcamp.com/album/the-story-of-jim-thorpe">The Story of Jim Thorpe</a>." Tall Paul is an Anishinaabe and Oneida Hip-Hop artist enrolled on the Leech Lake reservation in Minnesota. 
Biographer David Maraniss is the author of "<a href="https://bookshop.org/p/books/path-lit-by-lightning-the-life-of-jim-thorpe-david-maraniss/18501259?ean=9781476748412">Path Lit by Lightning: The Life of Jim Thorpe</a>."
Activist Suzan Shown Harjo is the recipient of a <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=28aiDWgxXdU">2014 Presidential Medal of Freedom</a>. She is Cheyenne and Hodulgee Muscogee.
Patty Loew is the director of the <a href="https://www.northwestern.edu/native-american-and-indigenous-peoples/people/cnair.html">Center for Native American and Indigenous Research</a> at Northwestern University. She is a member of the Bad River Band of Lake Superior Ojibwe.

        <![CDATA[<p>2019 was an important year throughout the African diaspora — the 400th year since enslaved Africans first arrived in the United States. In Ghana — once the center of the European slave trade — 2019 was declared "the year of return" and the start of a campaign to encourage descendants of enslaved Africans to re-connect with the land of their ancestors. Thousands of African-Americans made the trip to Ghana — and many have decided to stay. They're fed up with police brutality and systemic racism in the US, ready to build new lives in Africa — and their number is growing.</p>

        <![CDATA[<p>Rooted in reality, written with a keen observer’s eye, and shaped with a sense of song, documentary poetry tells the truth in an artist’s voice. So what are they writing about today?</p>

        <![CDATA[<p>Rooted in reality, written with a keen observer’s eye, and shaped with a sense of song, documentary poetry tells the truth in an artist’s voice. So what are they writing about today?</p>

        <![CDATA[<p>Do you ever feel like there’s something missing in your life? You don’t know exactly what it is. And there’s never enough time to really think about it.       <guid isPermaLink="false">prx_120_f45de908-191c-45ad-ad62-1450e001f6b7</guid>
      <title>Luminous: Can Psychedelics Be Decolonized?</title>
      <pubDate>Sat, 21 Oct 2023 11:00:00 -0000</pubDate>
      <link>https://www.ttbook.org/show/luminous-can-psychedelics-be-decolonized</link>
      <description>
        <![CDATA[<p>It’s easy to get caught up in the hype about how psychedelics might revolutionize the treatment of mental illness. But there are also lots of ethical concerns. And probably none are so troubling as the charges of exploitation and cultural appropriation. The fact is, the knowledge about many psychedelics — like magic mushrooms and ayahuasca — comes from the sacred ceremonies of Indigenous cultures. But over the past century, Western scientists and pharmaceutical companies have been going into these cultures, collecting plants and synthesizing their chemical compounds.</p>

<p>Even if science is all about building on the knowledge of earlier discoveries, what is the psychedelic industry's ethical responsibility? Can psychedelics be decolonized?</p>

<p><em>Original Air Date: October 21, 2023</em></p>

<p><strong>Interviews In This Hour:</strong></p>

<p><a href="https://www.ttbook.org/interview/tragic-story-maria-sabinas-sacred-mushrooms" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">The Tragic Story of Maria Sabina's Sacred Mushrooms </a>— <a href="https://www.ttbook.org/interview/empowering-indigenous-voices-psychedelic-industry" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">Empowering Indigenous voices in the psychedelic industry</a> — <a href="https://www.ttbook.org/interview/bioprospecting-psychedelics-how-pharma-hunted-indigenous-plant-medicines" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">Bioprospecting for psychedelics: How Pharma hunted for Indigenous plant medicines</a> — <a href="https://www.ttbook.org/interview/spirit-medicine-yuria-celidwens-vision-ethical-psychedelics" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">Spirit Medicine: Yuria Celidwen's vision for an ethical psychedelics</a></p>

<p><strong>Guests:</strong></p>

<p><a href="https://www.ttbook.org/people/michael-pollan" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">Michael Pollan</a>, <a href="https://www.ttbook.org/people/dennis-mckenna" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">Dennis McKenna</a>, <a href="https://www.ttbook.org/people/erika-dyck" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">Erika Dyck</a>, <a href="https://www.ttbook.org/people/katherine-maclean" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">Katherine MacLean</a>, <a href="https://www.ttbook.org/people/sutton-king" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">Sutton King</a>, <a href="https://www.ttbook.org/people/rachel-fernandez" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">Rachel Fernandez</a>, <a href="https://www.ttbook.org/people/lucas-richert" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">Lucas Richert</a>, <a href="https://www.ttbook.org/people/yuria-celidwen" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">Yuria Celidwen</a></p>

        <![CDATA[<p>Jim Thorpe was one of the greatest athletes the world has ever known — a legend in the NFL, MLB, NCAA, and in the Olympics. Today he is being celebrated by a new generation of Native Americans.</p>

<ul>
<li><p>Rapper Tall Paul’s album is called, “<a href="https://tallpaulhiphop.bandcamp.com/album/the-story-of-jim-thorpe" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">The Story of Jim Thorpe</a>." Tall Paul is an Anishinaabe and Oneida Hip-Hop artist enrolled on the Leech Lake reservation in Minnesota. </p></li>
<li><p>Biographer David Maraniss is the author of "<a href="https://bookshop.org/p/books/path-lit-by-lightning-the-life-of-jim-thorpe-david-maraniss/18501259?ean=9781476748412" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">Path Lit by Lightning: The Life of Jim Thorpe</a>."</p></li>
<li><p>Activist Suzan Shown Harjo is the recipient of a <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=28aiDWgxXdU" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">2014 Presidential Medal of Freedom</a>. She is Cheyenne and Hodulgee Muscogee.</p></li>
<li><p>Patty Loew is the director of the <a href="https://www.northwestern.edu/native-american-and-indigenous-peoples/people/cnair.html" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">Center for Native American and Indigenous Research</a> at Northwestern University. She is a member of the Bad River Band of Lake Superior Ojibwe.</p></li>
</ul>

      <title>Rethinking David Foster Wallace</title>
      <pubDate>Sat, 16 Sep 2023 11:00:00 -0000</pubDate>
      <link>https://www.ttbook.org/show/rethinking-david-foster-wallace</link>
      <description>
        <![CDATA[<p>Fifteen years ago, David Foster Wallace died by his own hand. He was a celebrated writer, but he now faces renewed criticism over his treatment of women, in his life and his books. After years of adulation, Wallace has become a symbol of lit-bro culture, and he's now facing a moment of reckoning. So how should we read him today?</p>

<p>This week, we talk with Wallace fans and critics. Many still consider him the greatest voice of his generation — even as they grapple with new details about his life. We also hear from Wallace himself — including a notable conversation he had with us on the eve of his greatest literary success.</p>

<p><em>Original Air Date: September 08, 2018</em></p>

<p><strong>Interviews In This Hour:</strong></p>

<p><strong>Guests:</strong></p>

<p><a href="https://www.ttbook.org/people/clare-hayes-brady" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">Clare Hayes-Brady</a>, <a href="https://www.ttbook.org/people/colleen-leahy" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">Colleen Leahy</a>, <a href="https://www.ttbook.org/people/makini-allwood" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">Makini Allwood</a>, <a href="https://www.ttbook.org/people/david-foster-wallace" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">David Foster Wallace</a>, <a href="https://www.ttbook.org/people/amy-wallace-havens" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">Amy Wallace-Havens</a></p>

      <title>Going for Broke: Making Up Our Minds</title>
      <pubDate>Sat, 02 Sep 2023 11:00:00 -0000</pubDate>
      <link>https://www.ttbook.org/show/going-broke-making-our-minds</link>
      <description>
        <![CDATA[<p><em>How we live is indelibly intertwined with the care and empathy we give to each other. What if we put care into helping Americans find homes and build dwellings, into keeping their bodies and minds sound, and finding meaningful and well-paid work? <a href="https://ttbook.org/goingforbroke" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">In this three part series</a>, "<a href="http://ttbook.org/" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">To The Best Of Our Knowledge</a>" and the <a href="http://economichardship.org/" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">Economic Hardship Reporting Project</a> bring you real life stories about economic struggle in our time, as well as ideas for solutions.</em></p>

<p>Post-traumatic stress disorder and other mental health challenges can push people into poverty. Meanwhile, the experience of financial desperation can also create even more trauma, even more suffering. How do you break the cycle? How do we truly care for people mentally and financially?</p>

<p><em>If you or someone you know are having mental health struggles, we wanted to make sure you are aware of some resources. <a href="https://nicic.gov/national-suicide-prevention-lifeline" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">The National Suicide and Crisis Lifeline</a> is available 24 hours a day by calling 9-8-8. <a href="https://www.nami.org/Home" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">The National Alliance on Mental Illness</a> reminds us that one in five people in the US has a mental health concern every year. You can find support and education at their web site, <a href="https://www.nami.org/Home" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">nami.org</a>.</em></p>

The satisfaction of gentle head scratches or a round of playing fetch is simple and pure, but in other ways, the connection we have is truly unknowable. How do dogs make our lives better? How do they think? And how do we give them the lives they deserve?</p>

      <title>Eye-To-Eye Animal Encounters</title>
      <pubDate>Sat, 27 May 2023 11:00:00 -0000</pubDate>
      <link>https://www.ttbook.org/show/eye-eye-animal-encounters</link>
      <description>
        <![CDATA[<p>There's a certain a kind of visual encounter that can be life changing: A cross-species gaze. The experience of looking directly into the eyes of an animal in the wild, and seeing it look back. It happens more often than you’d think and it can be so profound, there’s a name for it: eye-to-eye epiphany. So what happens when someone with feathers or fur and claws looks back? How does it change people, and what can it teach us?</p>

<p><em>Human identity cannot be separated from our nonhuman kin. From forest ecology to the human microbiome, emerging research suggests that being human is a complicated journey made possible only by the good graces of our many companions. In partnership with the <a href="http://humansandnature.org/kinship" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">Center for Humans and Nature</a> and with support from the <a href="https://kalliopeia.org/" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">Kalliopeia Foundation</a>, To The Best Of Our Knowledge is <a href="https://ttbook.org/kinship" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">exploring this theme of "kinship"</a> in a special radio series.</em></p>

<p><em>To learn more about the Kinship series, head to <a href="https://ttbook.org/kinship" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">ttbook.org/kinship</a>.</em></p>

<p><em>Original Air Date: February 08, 2020</em></p>

Thousands of African-Americans made the trip to Ghana — and many have decided to stay. They're fed up with police brutality and systemic racism in the US, ready to build new lives in Africa — and their number is growing.</p>

        <![CDATA[<p>Jim Thorpe was one of the greatest athletes the world has ever known — a legend in the NFL, MLB, NCAA, and in the Olympics. Today he is being celebrated by a new generation of Native Americans. </p>

<ul>
<li><p>Rapper Tall Paul’s album is called, “<a href="https://tallpaulhiphop.bandcamp.com/album/the-story-of-jim-thorpe" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">The Story of Jim Thorpe</a>." Tall Paul is an Anishinaabe and Oneida Hip-Hop artist enrolled on the Leech Lake reservation in Minnesota. </p></li>
<li><p>Biographer David Maraniss is the author of "<a href="https://bookshop.org/p/books/path-lit-by-lightning-the-life-of-jim-thorpe-david-maraniss/18501259?ean=9781476748412" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">Path Lit by Lightning: The Life of Jim Thorpe</a>."</p></li>
<li><p>Activist Suzan Shown Harjo is the recipient of a <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=28aiDWgxXdU" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">2014 Presidential Medal of Freedom</a>. She is Cheyenne and Hodulgee Muscogee.</p></li>
<li><p>Patty Loew is the director of the <a href="https://www.northwestern.edu/native-american-and-indigenous-peoples/people/cnair.html" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">Center for Native American and Indigenous Research</a> at Northwestern University. She is a member of the Bad River Band of Lake Superior Ojibwe.</p></li>
</ul>

      <title>When Mountains Are Gods</title>
      <pubDate>Sat, 24 Dec 2022 12:00:00 -0000</pubDate>
      <link>https://www.ttbook.org/show/when-mountains-are-gods</link>
      <description>
        <![CDATA[<p>If you look at a mountain, you might see a skiing destination, a climbing challenge, or even a source of timber to be logged or ore to be mined. But there was a time when mountains were sacred. In some places, they still are. What changes when you think of a mountain not as a giant accumulation of natural resources, but as a living being?</p>

<p><em>Human identity cannot be separated from our nonhuman kin. From forest ecology to the human microbiome, emerging research suggests that being human is a complicated journey made possible only by the good graces of our many companions. In partnership with the <a href="http://humansandnature.org/kinship" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">Center for Humans and Nature</a> and with support from the <a href="https://kalliopeia.org/" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">Kalliopeia Foundation</a>, To The Best Of Our Knowledge is <a href="https://ttbook.org/kinship" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">exploring this theme of "kinship"</a> in a special radio series.</em></p>

<p><em>To learn more about the Kinship series, head to <a href="https://ttbook.org/kinship" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">ttbook.org/kinship</a>.</em></p>

        <![CDATA[<p><em>How we live is indelibly intertwined with the care and empathy we give to each other. What if we put care into helping Americans find homes and build dwellings, into keeping their bodies and minds sound, and finding meaningful and well-paid work? <a href="https://ttbook.org/goingforbroke" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">In this three part series</a>, "<a href="http://ttbook.org/" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">To The Best Of Our Knowledge</a>" and the <a href="http://economichardship.org/" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">Economic Hardship Reporting Project</a> bring you real life stories about economic struggle in our time, as well as ideas for solutions.</em></p>

<p>Post-traumatic stress disorder and other mental health challenges can push people into poverty. Meanwhile, the experience of financial desperation can also create even more trauma, even more suffering. How do you break the cycle? How do we truly care for people mentally and financially?</p>

<p><em>If you or someone you know are having mental health struggles, we wanted to make sure you are aware of some resources. <a href="https://nicic.gov/national-suicide-prevention-lifeline" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">The National Suicide and Crisis Lifeline</a> is available 24 hours a day by calling 9-8-8. <a href="https://www.nami.org/Home" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">The National Alliance on Mental Illness</a> reminds us that one in five people in the US has a mental health concern every year. You can find support and education at their web site, <a href="https://www.nami.org/Home" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">nami.org</a>.</em></p>

      <title>Year of Return</title>
      <pubDate>Sat, 03 Sep 2022 11:00:00 -0000</pubDate>

      <description>
        <![CDATA[<p>2019 was an important year throughout the African diaspora — the 400th year since enslaved Africans first arrived in the United States. In Ghana — once the center of the European slave trade — 2019 was declared "the year of return" and the start of a campaign to encourage descendants of enslaved Africans to re-connect with the land of their ancestors. Thousands of African-Americans made the trip to Ghana — and many have decided to stay. They're fed up with police brutality and systemic racism in the US, ready to build new lives in Africa — and their number is growing.</p>

<p><em>Original Air Date: September 03, 2022</em></p>

      <title>The Secret Language of Trees</title>
      <pubDate>Sat, 27 Aug 2022 11:00:00 -0000</pubDate>

        <![CDATA[<p>Using a complex network of chemical signals, trees talk to each other and form alliances with fellow trees, even other species. And the root mass of aspens might live 100,000 years? We explore the science and history of trees and talk with Richard Powers about his epic novel "The Overstory."</p>

    <item>
      <guid isPermaLink="false">prx_120_45781ab9-da3c-4e7d-a0af-cf522ae114f5</guid>
      <title>Eye-To-Eye Animal Encounters</title>
      <pubDate>Sat, 20 Aug 2022 11:00:00 -0000</pubDate>
      <link>https://www.ttbook.org/show/eye-eye-animal-encounters</link>
      <description>
        <![CDATA[<p>There's a certain a kind of visual encounter that can be life changing: A cross-species gaze. The experience of looking directly into the eyes of an animal in the wild, and seeing it look back. It happens more often than you’d think and it can be so profound, there’s a name for it: eye-to-eye epiphany. So what happens when someone with feathers or fur and claws looks back? How does it change people, and what can it teach us?</p>

<p><em>Human identity cannot be separated from our nonhuman kin. From forest ecology to the human microbiome, emerging research suggests that being human is a complicated journey made possible only by the good graces of our many companions. In partnership with the <a href="http://humansandnature.org/kinship" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">Center for Humans and Nature</a> and with support from the <a href="https://kalliopeia.org/" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">Kalliopeia Foundation</a>, To The Best Of Our Knowledge is <a href="https://ttbook.org/kinship" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">exploring this theme of "kinship"</a> in a special radio series.</em></p>

        <![CDATA[There's a certain a kind of visual encounter that can be life changing: A cross-species gaze. The experience of looking directly into the eyes of an animal in the wild, and seeing it look back. It happens more often than you’d think and it can be so profound, there’s a name for it: eye-to-eye epiphany. So what happens when someone with feathers or fur and claws looks back? How does it change people, and what can it teach us?


Human identity cannot be separated from our nonhuman kin. From forest ecology to the human microbiome, emerging research suggests that being human is a complicated journey made possible only by the good graces of our many companions. In partnership with the <a href="http://humansandnature.org/kinship" target="_blank">Center for Humans and Nature</a> and with support from the <a href="https://kalliopeia.org/" target="_blank">Kalliopeia Foundation</a>, To The Best Of Our Knowledge is <a href="https://ttbook.org/kinship" target="_blank">exploring this theme of "kinship"</a> in a special radio series.

      <pubDate>Sat, 25 Jun 2022 11:00:00 -0000</pubDate>
      <link>https://www.ttbook.org/show/shapeshifting</link>
      <description>
        <![CDATA[<p>There are old folktales and legends of people who can become animals. Animals who can become people. And there’s a lesson for our own time in those shapeshifting stories — a recognition that the membrane between what's human and more-than-human is razor thin.</p>

<p><em>Human identity cannot be separated from our nonhuman kin. From forest ecology to the human microbiome, emerging research suggests that being human is a complicated journey made possible only by the good graces of our many companions. In partnership with the <a href="http://humansandnature.org/kinship" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">Center for Humans and Nature</a> and with support from the <a href="https://kalliopeia.org/" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">Kalliopeia Foundation</a>, To The Best Of Our Knowledge is <a href="https://ttbook.org/kinship" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">exploring this theme of "kinship"</a> in a special radio series.</em></p>

<p><em>To learn more about the Kinship series, head to <a href="https://ttbook.org/kinship" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">ttbook.org/kinship</a>.</em></p>

<p><em>Original Air Date: November 20, 2021</em></p>

<p><strong>Guests:</strong> </p>

<p><a href="https://www.ttbook.org/people/sharon-blackie" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">Sharon Blackie</a> — <a href="https://www.ttbook.org/people/david-abram" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">David Abram</a> — <a href="https://www.ttbook.org/people/chris-gosden" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">Chris Gosden</a> — <a href="https://www.ttbook.org/people/stephen-graham-jones" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">Stephen Graham Jones</a></p>

<p><strong>Interviews In This Hour:</strong> </p>

<p><a href="https://www.ttbook.org/interview/reclaiming-fierce-women-who-are-shapeshifters" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">Reclaiming the fierce women who are shapeshifters</a> — <a href="https://www.ttbook.org/interview/how-man-turned-raven" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">How a man turned into a raven</a> — <a href="https://www.ttbook.org/interview/shapeshifters-shamans-and-new-animism" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">Shapeshifters, shamans and the 'New Animism'</a> — <a href="https://www.ttbook.org/interview/horror-author-stephen-graham-jones-what-our-monsters-say-about-us" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">Horror author Stephen Graham Jones on what our monsters say about us</a></p>

How do they do it — and what can we learn from them?</p>

        <![CDATA[<p>If you had to travel 500 miles across country, on foot, with no map, no GPS, without talking to anyone — to a destination you've never seen, could you do it? It sounds impossible, but millions of creatures spend their lives on the move, migrating from one part of the Earth to another with navigation skills we can only dream of. How do they do it — and what can we learn from them?</p>

<p><em>Original Air Date: July 25, 2020</em></p>

      <title>Our Virtual Reality</title>
      <pubDate>Sat, 30 Apr 2022 11:00:00 -0000</pubDate>
      <link>https://www.ttbook.org/show/our-virtual-reality</link>
      <description>
        <![CDATA[<p>Not everyone has a nice, big yard to stretch out in while sheltering in place from COVID-19. But maybe you don't need one. People are using virtual spaces to live out the real experiences they miss — like coffee shops, road trips, even building your own house on a deserted island, or Walden Pond. In a world where we're mostly confined to our homes and Zoom screens, does the line between virtual and real-life space mean much anymore?</p>

    <item>
      <guid isPermaLink="false">prx_120_e26f71fb-9905-4e2d-8cba-b4e9f28f79ed</guid>
      <title>Plants As Persons</title>
      <pubDate>Sat, 16 Apr 2022 11:00:00 -0000</pubDate>
      <link>https://www.ttbook.org/show/plants-persons</link>
      <description>
        <![CDATA[<p>Over the past decade, plant scientists have quietly transformed the way we think of trees, forests and plants. They discovered that trees communicate through vast underground networks, that plants learn and remember. If plants are intelligent beings, how should we relate to them? Do they have a place in our moral universe? Should they have rights?</p>

<p><em>Human identity cannot be separated from our nonhuman kin. From forest ecology to the human microbiome, emerging research suggests that being human is a complicated journey made possible only by the good graces of our many companions. In partnership with the <a href="http://humansandnature.org/kinship" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">Center for Humans and Nature</a> and with support from the <a href="https://kalliopeia.org/" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">Kalliopeia Foundation</a>, To The Best Of Our Knowledge is <a href="https://ttbook.org/kinship" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">exploring this theme of "kinship"</a> in a special radio series.</em></p>

<p><em>To learn more about the Kinship series, head to <a href="https://ttbook.org/kinship" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">ttbook.org/kinship</a>.</em></p>

        <![CDATA[Over the past decade, plant scientists have quietly transformed the way we think of trees, forests and plants. They discovered that trees communicate through vast underground networks, that plants learn and remember. If plants are intelligent beings, how should we relate to them? Do they have a place in our moral universe? Should they have rights?


Human identity cannot be separated from our nonhuman kin. From forest ecology to the human microbiome, emerging research suggests that being human is a complicated journey made possible only by the good graces of our many companions. In partnership with the <a href="http://humansandnature.org/kinship" target="_blank">Center for Humans and Nature</a> and with support from the <a href="https://kalliopeia.org/" target="_blank">Kalliopeia Foundation</a>, To The Best Of Our Knowledge is <a href="https://ttbook.org/kinship" target="_blank">exploring this theme of "kinship"</a> in a special radio series.


To learn more about the Kinship series, head to <a href="https://ttbook.org/kinship" target="_blank">ttbook.org/kinship</a>.

      <title>When Mountains Are Gods</title>
      <pubDate>Sat, 12 Mar 2022 12:00:00 -0000</pubDate>
      <link>https://www.ttbook.org/show/when-mountains-are-gods</link>
      <description>
        <![CDATA[<p>If you look at a mountain, you might see a skiing destination, a climbing challenge, or even a source of timber to be logged or ore to be mined. But there was a time when mountains were sacred. In some places, they still are. What changes when you think of a mountain not as a giant accumulation of natural resources, but as a living being?</p>

<p><em>Human identity cannot be separated from our nonhuman kin. From forest ecology to the human microbiome, emerging research suggests that being human is a complicated journey made possible only by the good graces of our many companions. In partnership with the <a href="http://humansandnature.org/kinship" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">Center for Humans and Nature</a> and with support from the <a href="https://kalliopeia.org/" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">Kalliopeia Foundation</a>, To The Best Of Our Knowledge is <a href="https://ttbook.org/kinship" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">exploring this theme of "kinship"</a> in a special radio series.</em></p>

<p><em>Original Air Date: July 24, 2021</em></p>

In partnership with the <a href="http://humansandnature.org/kinship" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">Center for Humans and Nature</a> and with support from the <a href="https://kalliopeia.org/" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">Kalliopeia Foundation</a>, To The Best Of Our Knowledge is <a href="https://ttbook.org/kinship" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">exploring this theme of "kinship"</a> in a special radio series.</em></p>

<p><em>Original Air Date: July 24, 2021</em></p>

<p><strong>Guests:</strong> </p>

<p><a href="https://www.ttbook.org/people/john-hausdoerffer" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">John Hausdoerffer</a> — <a href="https://www.ttbook.org/people/regina-lopez-whiteskunk" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">Regina Lopez-Whiteskunk</a> — <a href="https://www.ttbook.org/people/david-hinton" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">David Hinton</a> — <a href="https://www.ttbook.org/people/lisa-maria-madera" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">Lisa Maria Madera</a></p>

<p><strong>Interviews In This Hour:</strong> </p>

      <title>Worshipping Waterfalls: The Evolution of Belief</title>
      <pubDate>Sat, 19 Feb 2022 12:00:00 -0000</pubDate>
      <link>https://www.ttbook.org/show/worshipping-waterfalls-evolution-belief</link>
      <description>
        <![CDATA[<p>Jane Goodall has seen wild chimpanzees dance and bristle with excitement around roaring waterfalls — and she thinks it’s an experience of awe and wonder — and possibly a precursor to animistic religion. </p>

<p>But can we ever know why our ancient human ancestors developed spiritual beliefs? Can evolutionary science uncover the roots of religion?  </p>

<p>At some point our ancestors went from admiring waterfalls to worshipping them - and all kinds of spirits and gods. They developed sacred rituals and turned stones into totems. And then came the Battle of the Gods. </p>

<p><em>This was produced in partnership with the Center for Humans and Nature, an organization that brings together scholars from a diversity of disciplines to think creatively about our relationships with nature and each other. What do you think evolution can tell us about love and morality? Share your thoughts at <a href="http://goo.gl/hUJMxr" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">humansandnature.org</a>. This episode was made possible through the support of the John Templeton Foundation.</em></p>

        <![CDATA[Jane Goodall has seen wild chimpanzees dance and bristle with excitement around roaring waterfalls — and she thinks it’s an experience of awe and wonder — and possibly a precursor to animistic religion. 


But can we ever know why our ancient human ancestors developed spiritual beliefs? Can evolutionary science uncover the roots of religion?  


At some point our ancestors went from admiring waterfalls to worshipping them - and all kinds of spirits and gods. They developed sacred rituals and turned stones into totems. And then came the Battle of the Gods. 


This was produced in partnership with the Center for Humans and Nature, an organization that brings together scholars from a diversity of disciplines to think creatively about our relationships with nature and each other. What do you think evolution can tell us about love and morality? Share your thoughts at <a href="http://goo.gl/hUJMxr" target="_blank">humansandnature.org</a>. This episode was made possible through the support of the John Templeton Foundation.

      <title>Our Time of Mourning</title>
      <pubDate>Sat, 29 Jan 2022 12:00:00 -0000</pubDate>
      <link>https://ttbook.org/show/our-time-mourning</link>
      <description>
        <![CDATA[<p>Is there a better way to talk about death? And to grieve? So many people have died during the pandemic — 4.8 million and counting — that we're living through a period of global mourning. And some people — and certain cultures — seem to be better prepared to handle it than others.</p>

      <title>A Parenting Revolution</title>
      <pubDate>Sat, 08 Jan 2022 12:00:00 -0000</pubDate>

      <description>
        <![CDATA[<p>The pandemic has made it clear that parents are walking a tightrope with no safety net.       <title>Jazz Migrations</title>
      <pubDate>Sat, 09 Oct 2021 11:00:00 -0000</pubDate>
      <link>https://www.ttbook.org/show/jazz-migrations</link>
      <description>
        <![CDATA[<p>Music crosses boundaries between traditional and modern, local and global, personal and political. Take jazz — a musical form born out of forced migration and enslavement. We typically think it originated in New Orleans and then spread around the world. But today, we examine an alternate history of jazz — one that starts in Africa, then crisscrosses the planet, following the movements of people and empires -- from colonial powers to grassroots revolutionaries to contemporary artists throughout the diaspora.</p>

<p>This history of jazz is like the music itself: fluid and improvisatory.  </p>

<p>In this hour, produced in partnership with the <a href="https://chcinetwork.org/" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">Consortium of Humanities Centers and Institutes (CHCI)</a> — a global consortium of 270 humanities centers and institutes — we hear how both African and African-American music have shaped the sound of the world today.</p>

<p> </p>

<p><em>Original Air Date: July 04, 2020</em></p>

        <![CDATA[<p>For all the commentary, the sorrow and rage, all the second-guessing about everything that followed, it’s still hard to fathom what happened on 9/11. Photographer James Nachtwey was in New York that day, and he took some of the iconic photos of the Twin Towers as they crumbled. "I’ve actually never gotten over it," he says. On the twentieth anniversary of 9/11, Nachtwey reflects on his life as a war photographer, and we consider the deep history of war itself. We also examine a very difficult question: Is war ever worth it?</p>

      <title>Traveling By Book</title>
      <pubDate>Sat, 04 Sep 2021 11:00:00 -0000</pubDate>
      <link>https://www.ttbook.org/show/traveling-book</link>
      <description>
        <![CDATA[<p>Before the time of commercial flights and road trips, we traveled to far off places without taking a single step. All you had to do was open a book. From Africa to England, to a kamikaze cockpit, and to realms of fantasy. Books aren’t just books. They’re passports to anywhere.</p>

        <![CDATA[<p>Over the past decade, plant scientists have quietly transformed the way we think of trees, forests and plants. They discovered that trees communicate through vast underground networks, that plants learn and remember. If plants are intelligent beings, how should we relate to them? Do they have a place in our moral universe? Should they have rights?</p>

<p><em>Human identity cannot be separated from our nonhuman kin. From forest ecology to the human microbiome, emerging research suggests that being human is a complicated journey made possible only by the good graces of our many companions. In partnership with the <a href="http://humansandnature.org/kinship" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">Center for Humans and Nature</a> and with support from the <a href="https://kalliopeia.org/" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">Kalliopeia Foundation</a>, To The Best Of Our Knowledge is <a href="https://ttbook.org/kinship" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">exploring this theme of "kinship"</a> in a special radio series.</em></p>

      <title>Writing the Climate Change Story</title>
      <pubDate>Sat, 14 Aug 2021 11:00:00 -0000</pubDate>

        <![CDATA[<p>If you look at a mountain, you might see a skiing destination, a climbing challenge, or even a source of timber to be logged or ore to be mined. But there was a time when mountains were sacred. In some places, they still are. What changes when you think of a mountain not as a giant accumulation of natural resources, but as a living being?</p>

<p><em>Today’s show is part of our project on kinship with the more-than-human world — produced in collaboration with the Center for Humans and Nature, and with support from the Kalliopeia Foundation. You’ll find more information about the project at <a href="http://ttbook.org/kinship" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">ttbook.org/kinship</a> and <a href="http://humansandnature.org" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">humansandnature.org</a>.</em></p>

<p><em>Original Air Date: July 24, 2021</em></p>

<p><strong>Guests:</strong></p>

      <title>How Africans Are Building The Cities Of The Future</title>
      <pubDate>Sat, 17 Jul 2021 19:08:34 -0000</pubDate>
      <link>https://www.ttbook.org/show/how-africans-are-building-cities-future</link>
      <description>
        <![CDATA[<p>Africans are moving into cities in unprecedented numbers. Lagos, Nigeria, is growing by 77 people an <em>hour</em> — it's on track to become a city of 100 million. In 30 years, the continent is projected to have 14 mega-cities of more than 10 million people. It's perhaps the largest urban migration in history.</p>

<p>These cities are not like Dubai, or Singapore, or Los Angeles. They’re uniquely African cities, and they’re forcing all of us to reconsider what makes a city modern. And how and why cities thrive.</p>

<p>To find out what's going on, we go to Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, to talk with entrepreneurs, writers, scholars and artists. In this hour, produced in partnership with the <a href="https://chcinetwork.org/" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">Consortium of Humanities Centers and Institutes (CHCI)</a> — a global consortium of 270 humanities centers and institutes — we learn how the continent where the human species was born is building the cities of the future.</p>

<p><em>Original Air Date: December 14, 2019</em></p>

<p><strong>Guests:</strong></p>

<p><a href="https://www.ttbook.org/people/dagmawi-woubshet" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">Dagmawi Woubshet</a> — <a href="https://www.ttbook.org/people/julie-mehretu" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">Julie Mehretu</a> — <a href="https://www.ttbook.org/people/emily-callaci" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">Emily Callaci</a> — <a href="https://www.ttbook.org/people/james-ogude" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">James Ogude</a> — <a href="https://www.ttbook.org/people/ato-qyayson" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">Ato Qyayson</a> — <a href="https://www.ttbook.org/people/teju-cole" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">Teju Cole</a> — <a href="https://www.ttbook.org/people/meskerem-assegued" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">Meskerem Assegued</a></p>

      <title>As Read By The Author</title>
      <pubDate>Sat, 03 Jul 2021 11:00:00 -0000</pubDate>
      <link>https://www.ttbook.org/show/read-author</link>
      <description>
        <![CDATA[<p>As audio producers, one of the most fun things we get to do is bring the soundscape of a novel to life — cue the monsters, the storms, the footsteps of a creature emerging slowly from the ocean. So that’s what we’re bringing you today: Great writers, epic sound design.</p>

<p><em>Original Air Date: July 03, 2021</em></p>

<p><strong>Guests:</strong></p>

<p><a href="https://www.ttbook.org/people/nnedi-okorafor" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">Nnedi Okorafor</a> — <a href="https://www.ttbook.org/people/neil-gaiman" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">Neil Gaiman</a> — <a href="https://www.ttbook.org/people/lidia-yuknavitch" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">Lidia Yuknavitch</a> — <a href="https://www.ttbook.org/people/n-k-jemisin" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">N. K.       <title>Eye-To-Eye Animal Encounters</title>
      <pubDate>Sat, 26 Jun 2021 11:00:00 -0000</pubDate>
      <link>https://www.ttbook.org/show/eye-eye-animal-encounters</link>
      <description>
        <![CDATA[<p>There's a certain a kind of visual encounter that can be life changing: A cross-species gaze. The experience of looking directly into the eyes of an animal in the wild, and seeing it look back. It happens more often than you’d think and it can be so profound, there’s a name for it: eye-to-eye epiphany. So what happens when someone with feathers or fur and claws looks back? How does it change people, and what can it teach us?</p>

<p><em>Human identity cannot be separated from our nonhuman kin. From forest ecology to the human microbiome, emerging research suggests that being human is a complicated journey made possible only by the good graces of our many companions. In partnership with the <a href="https://www.humansandnature.org/" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">Center for Humans and Nature</a> and with support from the <a href="https://kalliopeia.org/" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">Kalliopeia Foundation</a>, To The Best Of Our Knowledge is <a href="https://ttbook.org/kinship" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">exploring this theme of "kinship"</a> in a special radio series.</em></p>

<p><em>Original Air Date: February 08, 2020</em></p>

<p><strong>Guests:</strong></p>

<p><a href="https://www.ttbook.org/people/gavin-van-horn" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">Gavin Van Horn</a> — <a href="https://www.ttbook.org/people/jenny-kendler" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">Jenny Kendler</a> — <a href="https://www.ttbook.org/people/ivan-schwab" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">Ivan Schwab</a> — <a href="https://www.ttbook.org/people/jane-goodall" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">Jane Goodall</a> — <a href="https://www.ttbook.org/people/alan-lightman" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">Alan Lightman</a></p>

<p><strong>Interviews In This Hour:</strong></p>

A Brief Meditation</a> — <a href="https://www.ttbook.org/interview/sharing-eye-eye-epiphanies-animal-world" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">Sharing Eye-To-Eye Epiphanies With The Animal World</a></p>

      <content:encoded>
        <![CDATA[<p>Colonization in Africa was much more than a land grab. It was a project to replace — and even erase — local cultures. To label them inferior.       <title>Jazz Migrations</title>
      <pubDate>Sat, 06 Mar 2021 12:00:00 -0000</pubDate>
      <link>https://www.ttbook.org/show/jazz-migrations</link>
      <description>
        <![CDATA[<p>Music crosses boundaries between traditional and modern, local and global, personal and political. Take jazz — a musical form born out of forced migration and enslavement. We typically think it originated in New Orleans and then spread around the world. But today, we examine an alternate history of jazz — one that starts in Africa, then crisscrosses the planet, following the movements of people and empires — from colonial powers to grassroots revolutionaries to contemporary artists throughout the diaspora.</p>

<p>This history of jazz is like the music itself: fluid and improvisatory.  </p>

<p>In this hour, produced in partnership with the <a href="https://chcinetwork.org" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">Consortium of Humanities Centers and Institutes (CHCI)</a> — a global consortium of 270 humanities centers and institutes — we hear how both African and African-American music have shaped the sound of the world today.</p>

<p> </p>

<p><em>Original Air Date: July 04, 2020</em></p>

      <guid isPermaLink="false">prx_120_fccbcd1f-b5af-4d37-9fe9-3e88b9762b48</guid>
      <title>Plants As Persons</title>
      <pubDate>Sat, 19 Dec 2020 12:00:00 -0000</pubDate>
      <link>https://www.ttbook.org/show/plants-persons</link>
      <description>
        <![CDATA[<p>Over the past decade, plant scientists have quietly transformed the way we think of trees, forests and plants. They discovered that trees communicate through vast underground networks, that plants learn and remember. If plants are intelligent beings, how should we relate to them? Do they have a place in our moral universe? Should they have rights?</p>

<p><em>Human identity cannot be separated from our nonhuman kin. From forest ecology to the human microbiome, emerging research suggests that being human is a complicated journey made possible only by the good graces of our many companions. In partnership with the <a href="https://www.humansandnature.org/" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">Center for Humans and Nature</a> and with support from the <a href="https://kalliopeia.org/" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">Kalliopeia Foundation</a>, To The Best Of Our Knowledge is <a href="https://ttbook.org/kinship" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">exploring this theme of "kinship"</a> in a special radio series.</em></p>

<p><em>Original Air Date: December 19, 2020</em></p>

<p><strong>Guests:</strong></p>

<p><a href="https://www.ttbook.org/people/robin-wall-kimmerer" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">Robin Wall Kimmerer</a> — <a href="https://www.ttbook.org/people/matt-hall" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">Matt Hall</a> — <a href="https://www.ttbook.org/people/monica-gagliano" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">Monica Gagliano</a> — <a href="https://www.ttbook.org/people/brooke-hecht" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">Brooke Hecht</a></p>

        <![CDATA[<p>There's a certain a kind of visual encounter that can be life changing: A cross-species gaze. The experience of looking directly into the eyes of an animal in the wild, and seeing it look back. How does it change people, and what can it teach us?</p>

      <guid isPermaLink="false">prx_120_f540eaca-19cf-43c9-bfb4-42651173f139</guid>
      <title>How Africans Are Building The Cities Of The Future</title>
      <pubDate>Sat, 26 Sep 2020 11:01:00 -0000</pubDate>
      <link>https://www.ttbook.org/show/how-africans-are-building-cities-future</link>
      <description>
        <![CDATA[<p>Africans are moving into cities in unprecedented numbers. Lagos, Nigeria, is growing by 77 people an <em>hour</em> — it's on track to become a city of 100 million. In 30 years, the continent is projected to have 14 mega-cities of more than 10 million people. It's perhaps the largest urban migration in history.</p>

<p>These cities are not like Dubai, or Singapore, or Los Angeles. They’re uniquely African cities, and they’re forcing all of us to reconsider what makes a city modern. And how and why cities thrive.</p>

<p>To find out what's going on, we go to Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, to talk with entrepreneurs, writers, scholars and artists. In this hour, produced in partnership with the <a href="https://chcinetwork.org/" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">Consortium of Humanities Centers and Institutes (CHCI)</a> — a global consortium of 270 humanities centers and institutes — we learn how the continent where the human species was born is building the cities of the future.</p>

<p><em>Original Air Date: December 14, 2019</em></p>

<p><strong>Guests:</strong></p>

        <![CDATA[<p>Africans are moving into cities in unprecedented numbers. Lagos, Nigeria, is growing by 77 people an <em>hour</em> — it's on track to become a city of 100 million. In 30 years, the continent is projected to have 14 mega-cities of more than 10 million people. It's perhaps the largest urban migration in history.</p>

<p>These cities are not like Dubai, or Singapore, or Los Angeles. They’re uniquely African cities, and they’re forcing all of us to reconsider what makes a city modern. And how and why cities thrive.</p>

<p>To find out what's going on, we go to Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, to talk with entrepreneurs, writers, scholars and artists. In this hour, produced in partnership with the <a href="https://chcinetwork.org/" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">Consortium of Humanities Centers and Institutes (CHCI)</a> — a global consortium of 270 humanities centers and institutes — we learn how the continent where the human species was born is building the cities of the future.</p>

      <title>Loving Bees</title>
      <pubDate>Sat, 01 Aug 2020 11:00:00 -0000</pubDate>
      <link>https://www.ttbook.org/show/loving-bees</link>
      <description>
        <![CDATA[<p>Bees stir each one of our senses — the zen-like hum, the sweet honey, the waxy smell of wildflowers mixed with hard work, the vibrant orange and black bodies attached to window-paned wings. <br>
If they land on us, and we are calm, say beekeepers, it will be a gentle touch; they will sting only to save their lives. <br>
<br>
Bees are endangered, but all over the world, people are stepping up to save them — in backyards, science labs, and the abandoned lots of urban Detroit. We explore the art to building a relationship with bees, and the science of how they thrive and what we might do to preserve them for future generations.</p>

<p><em>Original Air Date: July 28, 2018</em></p>

      <title>Jazz Migrations</title>
      <pubDate>Fri, 03 Jul 2020 23:33:16 -0000</pubDate>
      <link>https://www.ttbook.org/show/jazz-migrations</link>
      <description>
        <![CDATA[<p>Music crosses boundaries between traditional and modern, local and global, personal and political. Take jazz — a musical form born out of forced migration and enslavement. We typically think it originated in New Orleans and then spread around the world. But today, we examine an alternate history of jazz — one that starts in Africa, then crisscrosses the planet, following the movements of people and empires -- from colonial powers to grassroots revolutionaries to contemporary artists throughout the diaspora.</p>

<p>This history of jazz is like the music itself: fluid and improvisatory.  </p>

<p>In this hour, produced in partnership with the <a href="https://chcinetwork.org/" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">Consortium of Humanities Centers and Institutes (CHCI)</a> — a global consortium of 270 humanities centers and institutes — we hear how both African and African-American music have shaped the sound of the world today.</p>

<p> </p>

      <title>Filtering Free Speech</title>
      <pubDate>Sat, 06 Jun 2020 11:05:00 -0000</pubDate>
      <link>https://www.ttbook.org/show/filtering-free-speech</link>
      <description>
        <![CDATA[<p>The line between free speech and hate speech isn't always clear. When college students shout down a campus speaker, when a woman yells racial slurs in a parking lot, or when HR calls with a reprimand — when does free speech violate safe space? When does sensitivity become censorship?</p>

<p><em>This weekend’s program "Filtering Free Speech" examines the difficult subject of censorship and free expression. In our first interview, acclaimed writer Walter Mosley uses the "N-word" four times to describe a very troubling experience when he was reprimanded for using this word in a Hollywood writers’ room. Mosley, who himself is black, was so angered by the exchange that he resigned from his job.</em></p>

<p><em>The "N-word" is intrinsic to his story — not gratuitous — so we have chosen not to bleep the word. On the broadcast our host provides a very clear warning to alert listeners to what they will hear.</em></p>

<p><em>If you'd prefer to listen to a censored version, <a href="https://www.ttbook.org/show/filtering-free-speech" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">you can listen to one here.</a></em></p>

      <guid isPermaLink="false">prx_120_19346b70-d7c7-4d3f-8322-d858bd5f7949</guid>
      <title>Who Owns Seeds?</title>
      <pubDate>Sat, 30 May 2020 11:04:00 -0000</pubDate>
      <link>https://www.ttbook.org/show/who-owns-seeds</link>
      <description>
        <![CDATA[<p>It's easy to take seeds for granted, to assume that there will always be more corn or wheat or rice to plant. But as monocropping and agribusiness continue to dominate modern farming, are we losing genetic diversity, cultural history, and the nutritional value of our food? We speak to farmers, botanists and indigenous people about how they are reclaiming our seeds.</p>

<p>*Original Air Date: *    <em>September 14, 2019</em></p>

<p>**Guests: **</p>

        <![CDATA[<p>This week, To the Best of Our Knowledge comes to you from our kitchens and homes. We’re safe, but we’ve all been thinking about the people on the front lines of the pandemic — doctors, nurses and hospital staffs. We’ve been seeing them on social media — the nurses in NYC wearing garbage bags because there aren’t enough<br>
sterile gowns.  Doctors figuring out those weird new face masks. Those incredibly brave doctors and nurses in Italy, Spain, France, the U.S. This hour we tell some remarkable stories of doctors and scientists who are saving lives.</p>

        <![CDATA[<p>Are there new ways to treat depression, anxiety and bipolar disorder? We explore some unconventional treatments for mental illness, including exercise, psychedelics and even horror films.</p>

      <guid isPermaLink="false">prx_120_ebe2f607-12ea-4203-bbf8-f730732e02ec</guid>
      <title>Listening to the City [Rebroadcast]</title>
      <pubDate>Sat, 11 May 2019 11:00:00 -0000</pubDate>
      <link>https://www.ttbook.org/show/listening-city</link>
      <description>
        <![CDATA[<p>Cities can be cacophonous and loud, a chaos of sonic discord. If, that is, you don't really focus your listening. People who’ve trained their ears to hear urban soundscapes in new ways hear something different.</p>

<p>That’s what David Rothenberg is doing. He’s a composer and an environmental philosopher who’s made a career of listening to and performing music in the wild, with birds, animals and insects. Lately he’s been giving himself a crash course in the art — and science — of urban listening.</p>

<p>His experience made us wonder: what else can you hear from a city when you really listen closely? People's patterns and everyday experiences emerge in detail, along with their struggles against prejudice and abuse. Some people hear pain, others hear art emerging from the chaos of sound.</p>

<p>In this hour, we make the case for exploring your city sonically.</p>

      <guid isPermaLink="false">prx_120_e55a0261-dfd9-47a6-bcaa-4218111f7360</guid>
      <title>The Secret Language of Trees [Rebroadcast]</title>
      <pubDate>Sat, 15 Dec 2018 11:00:00 -0000</pubDate>
      <link>https://www.ttbook.org/show/secret-language-trees</link>
      <description>
        <![CDATA[<p>Using a complex network of chemical signals, trees talk to each other and form alliances with fellow trees, even other species. In fact, whole forests exist as a kind of superorganism. And some trees are incredibly old. Did you know a single bristlecone pine can live up to 6,000 years? If you're looking for more in-depth knowledge on what you might be going through, <a href="https://www.nami.org/" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">the National Alliance on Mental Illness is an incredible resource.</a></p>

<p>And if you just need something to elevate your spirit, check out the playlist that Charles made at the bottom of this page. It's packed with the music he listens to when he’s down and needs a lift. Not a fake happy song kind of lift – something honest but also hopeful.</p>

<p><em>**WARNING: </em><em>The conversation with Lauren Slater in this show features frank discussion of depression and self-harm. The audio doesn't contain a trigger warning, but for listeners who may be sensitive to discussion of suicide, please consider listening to other interviews on the show separately, or skipping this episode.</em></p>

We live, work and play in Red and Blue tribal bubbles, filling our social media feeds with news sources that affirm our place in that order, rather than challenging it. That isolation is breeding an ugly, seething hatred of the other side that feels poisonous and dispiriting. So what can we do? In this hour, we hear how conservative talk show host Charlie Sykes lost his faith in the GOP and why a former CEO of NPR left his liberal bubble. Also, how Black Twitter has created its own safe space.</p>

        <![CDATA[<p>Ever had the nagging suspicion that you’re being watched? You are.  We all are.  Surrounded by security cameras — in malls, restaurants, airports, workplaces, even in church, spied on by our very own phones and computers. Yes, surveillance can keep us safe, but we’re in danger of losing the last shreds of our privacy. In this hour, we explore not only the pros and cons of living while being watched, but what it's like to be doing the watching.</p>

<p>Guests: <br>
<a href="https://www.ttbook.org/people/cari-ness-nesje" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">Cari Ness Nesje<br>
</a><a href="https://www.ttbook.org/people/randolph-lewis" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">Randolph Lewis<br>
</a><a href="https://www.ttbook.org/people/lily-hay-newman" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">Lily Hay Newman<br>
</a><a href="https://www.ttbook.org/people/josh-koury" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">Josh Koury<br>
</a><a href="https://www.ttbook.org/people/myles-kane" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">Myles Kane<br>
</a><a href="https://www.ttbook.org/people/marina-lutz" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">Marina Lutz</a></p>

<h3><strong><a href="https://www.ttbook.org/interview/who-else-siri-talking" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">Who Else Is Siri Talking To?</a></strong></h3>

<p>Do you ever get the feeling that your digital devices are eavesdropping on you?</p>

<h3><a href="https://www.ttbook.org/interview/life-beneath-electric-eyes" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">Life Beneath the Electric Eyes</a></h3>

<p>The personal devices we live with and depend on — our computers, tablets, smartphones and more— all share information about us. Randolph Lewis tells more stories about how we’re being watched in a book called “Under Surveillance.”</p>

<h3><a href="https://www.ttbook.org/interview/taking-back-control-over-whos-tapped-watch-us" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">Taking Back Control Over Who's Tapped In To Watch Us</a></h3>

<p>In a world filled with devices that could be used to listen in on our daily lives, how do you take back control of your privacy? Steve Paulson asked security reporter Lily Hay Newman.</p>

<h3><a href="https://www.ttbook.org/interview/innkeeper-hidden-walls" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">The Innkeeper Hidden In The Walls</a></h3>

<p>A couple of years ago, journalist Gay Talese published “The Voyeur’s Motel,” the true story of a motel owner who spent more than 30 years spying on his guests while they had sex. The case is now the subject of a Netflix documentary called “Voyeur.”</p>

<h3><strong><a href="https://www.ttbook.org/interview/when-family-photos-go-too-far" rel="nofollow" target="_blank">When Family Photos Go Too Far</a></strong></h3>

<p>Marina Lutz grew up with a father who was obsessed with watching her. She discovered the full extent of his obsession as an adult, and made an award-winning short documentary about it called “The Marina Experiment.”</p>]]>

      <pubDate>Sat, 06 Jan 2018 12:00:00 -0000</pubDate>

      <description>
        <![CDATA[<p>Ah, January.  Season of diets and fasts and cleanses, of "Drynuary" and "Veganuary."  Why does being virtuous always seem to mean giving up pleasure?  This hour, we explore the concept of renunciation and our complicated feelings about it.
